## Commit to a Prediction {.quiz-question .prompt-slide}

A $10\,M_\odot$ star has about $10\times$ the Sun's fuel
but about $3000\times$ the Sun's luminosity.

Its lifetime should be:

- about $10\times$ longer
- about the same
- [about $300\times$ shorter]{.correct}
- impossible to predict without a full stellar model

::: {.fragment .mini-note}
Target idea: lifetime = available energy / burn rate.
:::

## {.center}

Every Star Is a Clock
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Mass sets the fuel supply.
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}

## The Lifetime Logic

$$
\tau
\sim
\frac{\text{fuel}}{\text{burn rate}}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
More mass → more fuel
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
More mass → MUCH higher luminosity
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Burn rate wins.
:::

---

## Why Normalize to the Sun?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Ratio method**

1. Write the star equation.
2. Write the solar equation.
3. Divide.
4. Cancel shared units.
5. Read the scaling.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Given:** $M = 2\,M_\odot$, $L = 10\,L_\odot$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Want:** $\dfrac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Solar-Normalized Example: Show the Algebra

::: {.fragment}
$$
\frac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}
\approx
\left(\frac{2\,\cancel{M_\odot}}{1\,\cancel{M_\odot}}\right)
\left(\frac{10\,\cancel{L_\odot}}{1\,\cancel{L_\odot}}\right)^{-1}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
= 2 \times 10^{-1} = 0.2
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
This star gets only 20% of the Sun's main-sequence lifetime.
:::

---

## Clock 1: Dynamical Response

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
{{< include ../../../_includes/equations/dynamical-timescale.qmd >}}
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.incremental .text-sm}
- structural response clock
- set mainly by **mean density**
- **not** the age of the star
:::
:::
::::

---

## Mean Density Is the Compactness Shortcut

$$
\bar{\rho} = \frac{3M}{4\pi R^3}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
smaller radius at fixed mass → larger density
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
larger density → shorter dynamical time
:::

---

## Solar-Normalized Dynamical Clock

$$
\frac{\tau_{\text{dyn}}}{\tau_{\text{dyn},\odot}}
=
\left(\frac{\bar{\rho}}{\bar{\rho}_\odot}\right)^{-1/2}
=
\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{-1/2}
\left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^{3/2}
$$

::: {.fragment .mini-note}
$G$ cancels, so the ratio keeps only the physics that changes from star to star.
:::

---

## For the Sun, the Response Time Is Shockingly Short

::: {.result-line}
$$
\tau_{\text{dyn},\odot} \approx 3 \times 10^3\,\text{s}
$$
:::

::: {.result-big}
50 minutes
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Structural imbalances get corrected very quickly.
:::

---

## Clock 2 Setup: The Gravitational Energy Reservoir

$$
E_{\text{grav}} \sim \frac{GM^2}{R}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
More mass → deeper gravitational well
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Larger radius → weaker binding
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
This is the energy gravity can release if the star contracts.
:::

---

## Luminosity Is the Energy Loss Rate

$$
L = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Luminosity is power.
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
It tells us how fast the star is losing energy.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\text{timescale}
\sim
\frac{\text{available energy}}{\text{energy loss rate}}
$$
:::

---

## Clock 2: The Kelvin-Helmholtz Timescale

::: {.fragment}
$$
\tau_\text{KH}
\sim
\frac{E_{\text{grav}}}{L}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\tau_\text{KH}
\sim
\frac{GM^2}{RL}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Gravity-only lifetime = gravitational reservoir / luminosity.
:::

---

## For the Sun, Gravity Lasts Only

::: {.result-line}
$$
\tau_{\text{KH},\odot} \approx 3 \times 10^7\,\text{yr}
$$
:::

::: {.result-big}
30 million years
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Gravity alone cannot power the Sun for billions of years.
:::

---

## Solar-Normalized Thermal Clock

$$
\frac{\tau_{\text{KH}}}{\tau_{\text{KH},\odot}}
=
\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^2
\left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^{-1}
\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^{-1}
$$

::: {.incremental .mini-list}
- more mass → more binding energy
- larger radius → weaker binding
- larger luminosity → faster spending
:::

---

## Quick Check: Burn Rate Still Matters {.quiz-question .prompt-slide}

Keep $M$ and $R$ fixed, but double $L$.

The Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale becomes:

- [half as long]{.correct}
- twice as long
- unchanged
- impossible to tell

## The Kelvin Problem

Kelvin's model gave the Sun only **tens of Myr**.

::: {.incremental .center-note}
Geology needed much more time.
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Biology needed much more time.
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The model was missing a deeper energy source.
:::

---

## Kelvin vs. the Geologists

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why Kelvin sounded reasonable**

::: {.incremental .text-sm}
- careful energy bookkeeping
- gravity really does release energy
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why Kelvin failed**

::: {.incremental .text-sm}
- the reservoir was too small
- fusion supplied the missing budget
:::
:::
::::

---

## Why $E = mc^2$ Changes the Budget

{{< img emc2-stellar-power width="86%" >}}

$$
\Delta E = \Delta m\,c^2
$$

::: {.fragment .mini-note}
Fusion taps rest-mass energy, not just thermal or chemical energy.
:::

---

## Clock 3: The True Main-Sequence Clock

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
{{< include ../../../_includes/equations/nuclear-timescale.qmd >}}
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.incremental .text-sm}
- $\varepsilon$: fusion efficiency
- $f_M$: accessible fuel fraction
- $L$: burn rate
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Now the Sun can last billions of years.
:::

---

## Full Normalized Nuclear Clock

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}
\approx\;&
\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_\odot}\right)
\left(\frac{f_M}{f_{M,\odot}}\right)
\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right) \\
&\times
\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment .mini-note}
$\varepsilon$ is similar for H $\rightarrow$ He fusion, but $f_M$ can vary.
:::

---

## Solar-Normalized Nuclear Clock

$$
\frac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}
\approx
\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)
\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^{-1}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Fuel in the numerator
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
Burn rate in the denominator
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The core competition is still fuel / burn rate.
:::

---

## For the Sun, the Nuclear Clock Is

::: {.result-line}
$$
\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot} \approx 10^{10}\,\text{yr}
$$
:::

::: {.result-big}
10 billion years
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
That is why fusion solves Kelvin's age problem.
:::

---

## Worked Example: A Fully Convective M Dwarf

::: {.fragment}
**Given:** $M = 0.2\,M_\odot$, $L \approx 0.008\,L_\odot$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Given:** $f_M \approx 10\,f_{M,\odot}$ for a fully convective star
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Want:** $\dfrac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}$
:::

::: {.fragment .mini-note}
Set up the ratios first so the algebra has somewhere to go.
:::

---

## M-Dwarf Lifetime: The Result

::: {.fragment}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\tau_{\text{nuc}}}{\tau_{\text{nuc},\odot}}
&\approx
\left(\frac{\cancel{\varepsilon}}{\cancel{\varepsilon_\odot}}\right)
\left(\frac{10\,\cancel{f_{M,\odot}}}{1\,\cancel{f_{M,\odot}}}\right)
\left(\frac{0.2\,\cancel{M_\odot}}{1\,\cancel{M_\odot}}\right)
\left(\frac{0.008\,\cancel{L_\odot}}{1\,\cancel{L_\odot}}\right)^{-1} \\
&= 10 \times 0.2 \times \frac{1}{0.008} \approx 250
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .result-big}
250 $\tau_\odot$
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Low-mass stars can outlive the current universe by orders of magnitude.
:::

---

## Fast Scaling Derivation

::: {.fragment}
$$
\tau \sim \frac{\text{fuel}}{\text{burn rate}}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\tau \sim \frac{M}{L}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
L \propto M^{3.5}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$
\tau \propto M^{-2.5}
$$
:::

---

## Why Massive Stars Die Young

$$
\frac{\tau_{\text{MS}}}{\tau_{\text{MS},\odot}}
\approx
\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{-2.5}
$$

::: {.fragment .center-note}
More mass → more fuel
:::

::: {.fragment .center-note}
More mass → MUCH higher luminosity
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Extra fuel does not keep up.
:::

---

## The Scaling That Explains the HR Diagram

::: {.clean-table}
| Mass | Main-sequence lifetime |
|:---:|:---:|
| $0.3\,M_\odot$ | longer than the age of the universe |
| $1\,M_\odot$ | $\sim 10\,\text{Gyr}$ |
| $2\,M_\odot$ | $\sim 2\,\text{Gyr}$ |
| $10\,M_\odot$ | $\sim 30\,\text{Myr}$ |
:::
